newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's right licks wounds over election defeat.
newsitem.headline: Iran's right licks wounds over election defeat.

text.p: Iran's conservative Islamic establishment publicly licked its wounds on Sunday after its worst electoral defeat in 18 years of revolution.

In a dramatic political about-face a majority of the Majlis or parliament dominated by conservatives loyal to the main loser in Friday's presidential election swung behind the victor with a public display of support.
But one of the right's main mouthpieces presented moderate clergyman Mohammad Khatami's landslide electoral triumph as votes for Islam and revolution rather than an individual.

Khatami's drubbing of conservatives through a mass turnout by a curious coalition of centrists, Islamist left-wingers, women, students, youths and intellectuals seeking change was Iran's biggest political upset since 1979 when fundamentalist Shi'ite Moslem clergymen led by the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini toppled the pro-American Shah.
At the first session of the 270-seat assembly since it was closed two weeks ago for the election campaign, more than 200 deputies sent a message to Khatami pledging full cooperation.

"No doubt this great epic is a reinforcement of the ideals of the late Imam Khomeini and a renewal of allegiance with the supreme leader of the Islamic revolution, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei," they said in a statement read in open session.
Nearly 200 deputies had supported Khatami's conservative rival, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, in the campaign while only 70 backed Khatami.
But Khatami won by a landslide -- 69 percent of a huge turnout of more than 29 million of Iran's 33 million electorate -- and trounced the speaker, who had to settle for 25 percent.
The defeated Nateq-Nouri said the massive turnout had surprised Western analysts and henceforth the Majlis would be an ally to Khatami and his government.
Khatami, in his first public comment since the election, said he hoped he could prove he deserved such popular support.
All groups should participate in making a prosperous, free and independent Iran, he said in a statement broadcast by Tehran radio which also stressed the rule of law.
Khamenei met Khatami for the first time since the election and gave him "appropriate guidelines", the official news agency IRNA reported.
The presidency is revolutionary Iran's highest elective office but ranks second to that of the supreme leader, who determines policy and whose word is sacrosanct.

President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, due to stand down in August after the maximum two four-year terms of office permitted by law, congratulated Khatami and urged government officials and clergy to back him.
Rafsanjani will continue to exercise powerful influence as head of a council of advisers which mediates any dispute between parliament and another body of clerics and lawyers.
At a two-hour news conference he said the election had shown that the Iranian people were more politicised and aware. The growth of understanding among people spoke good news of social development.

But Kayhan, the hardline Persian daily newspaper which speaks for the conservative establishment, said: "The 20 million votes Mr Khatami gathered were votes for the protection of Islam and revolution and no-one can claim otherwise".
It relegated news of the election to third place after a speech by Khamenei and Rafsanjani's news conference.
In a toughly-worded editorial Kayhan said the huge number of votes might lead to a feeling among excited supporters that they did not need guidance and criticism.
English daily Iran News said: "There was once a time when it was popularly believed that the sky would fall on the day the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, the late Imam Khomeini, ceased to live."
But he had died and one of his closest disciples, Khamenei, had filled the gap. It said the election confirmed that a philosophy, not a person, was the basis of the Islamic system.
